prompt:
You are a senior associate at a federal criminal defense firm. Your supervising partner, Zachary Ayers, represented Vincent Petrushkin in his appeal before the Ninth Circuit. The court has now vacated the sentence and remanded for resentencing. The partner has asked you to prepare a sentencing memorandum for the resentencing hearing before Judge Thomas O. Rice in the Eastern District of Washington.

The district court originally applied U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1) to calculate a Guidelines range of 110-120 months. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit in United States v. Petrushkin, 142 F.4th 1241 (9th Cir. 2025), held that mere possession of a firearm is insufficient to trigger the (c)(1) enhancement, and that the district court abused its discretion because it focused solely on Petrushkin's knowledge that his codefendant Randy Holmes intended to commit a robbery, without finding that Petrushkin possessed the firearm in a manner that potentially emboldened or facilitated Holmes's offense.

You must prepare a sentencing memorandum arguing for a sentence of time served, consistent with the defense's original request at the prior sentencing hearing. The memorandum should argue that the (c)(1) enhancement does not apply, that the alternative (b)(6)(B) enhancement should not be applied or should result in a significantly lower sentence, and that the 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) factors support a sentence of time served.

Materials provided:
- The Ninth Circuit opinion in United States v. Petrushkin, 142 F.4th 1241 (9th Cir. 2025), which contains the full factual background, the court's legal holdings regarding the scope of the appeal waiver, the application of § 2K2.1(c)(1), and the 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' standard from United States v. Routon, 25 F.3d 815 (9th Cir. 1994).

Prepare a sentencing memorandum in Word format that:
1. Identifies the correct legal standard for applying U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1) and (b)(6)(B) based on the Ninth Circuit's holding
2. Argues that the (c)(1) enhancement is inapplicable because Petrushkin's five-second possession of the firearm did not potentially embolden or facilitate Holmes's robbery
3. Addresses whether the (b)(6)(B) enhancement should apply and, if so, argues for the lower Guidelines range
4. Argues that the § 3553(a) factors support a sentence of time served
5. Cites the relevant legal authorities identified in the Ninth Circuit opinion, including United States v. Routon, 25 F.3d 815 (9th Cir. 1994); United States v. Holt, 510 F.3d 1007 (9th Cir. 2007); Gall v. United States, 552 U.S. 38 (2007); and United States v. Carty, 520 F.3d 984 (9th Cir. 2008)

The memorandum should be no more than 8 pages, use standard legal memorandum formatting with section headings, and include a signature block for Zachary L. Ayers, Ayers Law Firm PLLC, Spokane, Washington.

sections.heading: SENTENCING MEMORANDUM
required_content: Case caption: United States v. Vincent Nicholas Petrushkin, No. 2:21-cr-00164-TOR-2
Court identification: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington
Judge identification: Thomas O. Rice, District Judge
paragraphs:
IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF WASHINGTON

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,

Plaintiff,

v.

VINCENT NICHOLAS PETRUSHKIN,
AKA Vincint Petrushkin,
AKA Vincent Petrushkin,

Defendant.

Case No. 2:21-cr-00164-TOR-2

SENTENCING MEMORANDUM

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
required_content: Reference to Ninth Circuit vacatur and remand for resentencing
Identification of counsel: Zachary L. Ayers, Ayers Law Firm PLLC
Statement of requested sentence: time served
Brief summary of arguments
paragraphs: Defendant Vincent Nicholas Petrushkin, by and through undersigned counsel, respectfully submits this sentencing memorandum in advance of resentencing. The Ninth Circuit vacated Mr. Petrushkin's sentence and remanded for resentencing in United States v. Petrushkin, 142 F.4th 1241 (9th Cir. 2025), holding that the district court abused its discretion in applying the U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1) enhancement. As set forth below, the defense respectfully requests that the Court impose a sentence of time served.

As the Ninth Circuit explained, the district court's application of the (c)(1) enhancement was an abuse of discretion because the court 'focused solely on Petrushkin's knowledge that Holmes was going to commit a robbery' and 'did not find that Petrushkin possessed the firearm in a manner that potentially emboldened or facilitated Holmes's offense.' 142 F.4th at 1243. The defense submits that neither the (c)(1) enhancement nor the alternative (b)(6)(B) enhancement should apply to Mr. Petrushkin's case, and that even if an enhancement applies, the totality of the circumstances warrants a sentence of time served.

sections.heading: II. LEGAL STANDARD FOR U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1) AND (b)(6)(B)
required_content: Text of § 2K2.1(c)(1): cross-reference provision allowing courts to apply base level from another substantive offense if defendant used or possessed firearm in connection with another offense or with knowledge/intent it would be used in connection with another offense
Ninth Circuit's holding that Routon's 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' requirement applies to both clauses of § 2K2.1(c)(1)
Citation to United States v. Routon, 25 F.3d 815 (9th Cir. 1994)
Standard of review: de novo for legal interpretation of Sentencing Guidelines (citing United States v. Holt, 510 F.3d 1007, 1010 (9th Cir. 2007))
paragraphs: The Ninth Circuit reviewed the district court's legal interpretation of the Sentencing Guidelines de novo, citing United States v. Holt, 510 F.3d 1007, 1010 (9th Cir. 2007). 142 F.4th at 1246. The court held that the 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' requirement set forth in United States v. Routon, 25 F.3d 815 (9th Cir. 1994), applies to both clauses of § 2K2.1(c)(1). Id. at 1243.

Under § 2K2.1(c)(1), the enhancement applies if 'the defendant used or possessed any firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction in connection with the commission or attempted commission of another offense, or possessed or transferred a firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction with knowledge or intent that it would be used or possessed in connection with another offense.' Under the Routon standard, 'the government must show that the defendant possessed the firearm in a manner that potentially emboldened or facilitated the other offense.' 142 F.4th at 1243.

The alternative enhancement under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) applies when a defendant 'used or possessed any firearm or ammunition in connection with another felony offense; or possessed or transferred any firearm or ammunition with knowledge, intent, or reason to believe that it would be used or possessed in connection with another felony offense.' The defense submits that even if the (b)(6)(B) enhancement applies, the facts of this case warrant the lower Guidelines range.

sections.heading: III. THE § 2K2.1(c)(1) ENHANCEMENT DOES NOT APPLY
required_content: Facts: Petrushkin possessed the gun for approximately five seconds
Facts: Petrushkin held the gun, looked at it, said 'hell yeah,' and handed it back to Holmes
Facts: Holmes told Burns and Petrushkin he was 'gonna do this by myself homie' and rejected their offers of help
Ninth Circuit holding that district court focused solely on knowledge without finding possession emboldened or facilitated Holmes's offense
Ninth Circuit statement that facts do not permit the necessary inference
paragraphs: The Ninth Circuit has definitively held that the district court abused its discretion in applying the (c)(1) enhancement. The court found that the district court 'focused solely on Petrushkin's knowledge that Holmes was going to commit a robbery' and 'did not find that Petrushkin possessed the firearm in a manner that potentially emboldened or facilitated Holmes's offense.' 142 F.4th at 1243.

The facts of this case simply do not support application of the (c)(1) enhancement. As the Ninth Circuit explained, Petrushkin 'held the gun, looked at it and said hell yeah,' then 'handed the gun back to Holmes' and 'got into the backseat of the car.' 142 F.4th at 1244. Petrushkin possessed the gun for 'approximately five seconds.' Id. This fleeting possession was entirely passive and did not in any way embolden or facilitate Holmes's subsequent robbery of the undercover ATF agent.

Moreover, Holmes explicitly told Burns and Petrushkin that he was 'gonna do this by myself homie' and 'rejected their offers of help.' Id. Holmes intended to act alone, and Petrushkin's momentary handling of the firearm played no role in facilitating or emboldening Holmes's decision to commit the robbery or the robbery itself. The Ninth Circuit confirmed that 'the facts in the record' do not 'permit the necessary inference' that Petrushkin's possession emboldened or facilitated Holmes's offense. Id. at 1243.

Accordingly, the (c)(1) enhancement should not apply at resentencing. The government cannot satisfy the Routon standard because there is no evidence that Petrushkin's five-second handling of the firearm had any potential to embolden or facilitate the robbery committed by Holmes.

sections.heading: IV. THE (b)(6)(B) ENHANCEMENT AND GUIDELINES CALCULATION
required_content: Prior plea agreement recommended (b)(6)(B) enhancement
Prior Guidelines range with (b)(6)(B): 77 to 96 months
Prior Guidelines range with (c)(1): 110 to 120 months
Government's sentencing request: 12 months and one day
Defense's prior request: time served plus ten to twenty days
paragraphs: At the prior sentencing, the district court calculated an alternative Guidelines range of 77 to 96 months under the (b)(6)(B) enhancement, compared to 110 to 120 months under the (c)(1) enhancement. The plea agreement itself recommended a four-level increase under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B). The defense submits that even if the Court applies the (b)(6)(B) enhancement, the resulting Guidelines range should be the starting point for the Court's analysis, and the § 3553(a) factors strongly support a below-Guidelines sentence of time served.

Notably, the government itself requested a sentence of only 12 months and one day at the prior sentencing, which represents a substantial variance from even the lower Guidelines range of 77 to 96 months. The government's own recommendation reflects a recognition that the Guidelines ranges calculated in this case overstate the seriousness of Mr. Petrushkin's conduct.

sections.heading: V. THE § 3553(a) FACTORS SUPPORT A SENTENCE OF TIME SERVED
required_content: Reference to § 3553(a) factors
Argument regarding nature and circumstances of the offense
Argument regarding history and characteristics of the defendant
Argument regarding need for sentence to reflect seriousness of offense, promote respect for law, and provide just punishment
Argument regarding need for deterrence
Argument regarding need to protect the public
Argument regarding kinds of sentences available
Reference to Gall v. United States, 552 U.S. 38 (2007) and United States v. Carty, 520 F.3d 984 (9th Cir. 2008)
paragraphs: Under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a), the Court must consider the nature and circumstances of the offense, the history and characteristics of the defendant, the need for the sentence to reflect the seriousness of the offense, promote respect for law, provide just punishment, afford adequate deterrence, and protect the public. The Supreme Court has instructed in Gall v. United States, 552 U.S. 38, 51 (2007), that calculating the incorrect Guidelines range constitutes procedural error, and that the Guidelines are merely one factor among many.

The nature and circumstances of this offense strongly favor a sentence of time served. Mr. Petrushkin's conduct consisted of a single, five-second handling of a firearm that was immediately returned to the owner. He did not use the firearm in any criminal manner. He did not participate in the robbery that Holmes committed. Indeed, Holmes expressly rejected Petrushkin's offer to help. Mr. Petrushkin's involvement in this offense was minimal and peripheral.

The Ninth Circuit in United States v. Carty, 520 F.3d 984, 993 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc), instructed courts to 'consider the totality of the circumstances, including the degree of variance for a sentence imposed outside the Guidelines range' when evaluating substantive reasonableness. Here, even the government recognized that a significant variance from the Guidelines was appropriate by requesting only 12 months and one day. The defense submits that the totality of the circumstances warrants an even greater variance to time served.

A sentence of time served would adequately reflect the seriousness of Mr. Petrushkin's offense while accounting for the minimal nature of his conduct. Mr. Petrushkin has already served significant time in custody, and further incarceration would be disproportionate to his culpability. A sentence of time served would also promote respect for the law by ensuring that the punishment fits the conduct, rather than imposing a sentence inflated by inapplicable enhancements.

The need for deterrence is adequately addressed by the conviction itself and the time Mr. Petrushkin has already served. The public safety concern is minimal given that Mr. Petrushkin's conduct did not involve violence or any active participation in criminal activity beyond the brief handling of the firearm. The defense respectfully requests that the Court impose a sentence of time served, plus ten to twenty days to allow Mr. Petrushkin to finalize a community reentry plan, consistent with the defense's original request at the prior sentencing.

sections.heading: VI. CONCLUSION
required_content: Summary of arguments
Request for sentence of time served plus ten to twenty days
paragraphs: For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that the Court impose a sentence of time served, plus ten to twenty days to allow Mr. Petrushkin to finalize a community reentry plan. The Ninth Circuit has held that the (c)(1) enhancement does not apply to Mr. Petrushkin's case, and the § 3553(a) factors overwhelmingly support a sentence of time served.

# Seed Material: United States v. Petrushkin
Source: courtlistener
Identifier: cluster:10632484

Case Name: United States v. Petrushkin
Citation: 142 F.4th 1241
Court: ca9
Date Filed: 2025-07-14
Judges: None

## Opinion Text
FOR PUBLICATION UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, No. 23-572 D.C. No. Plaintiff - Appellee, 2:21-cr-00164- TOR-2 v. VINCENT NICHOLAS PETRUSHKIN, AKA Vincint OPINION Petrushkin, AKA Vincent Petrushkin, Defendant - Appellant. Appeal from the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington Thomas O. Rice, District Judge, Presiding Argued and Submitted September 11, 2024 Seattle, Washington Filed July 14, 2025 Before: William A. Fletcher and Jennifer Sung, Circuit Judges, and Jed S. Rakoff, District Judge. * Opinion by Judge Sung * The Honorable Jed S. Rakoff, United States District Judge for the Southern District of New York, sitting by designation. 2 USA V. PETRUSHKIN SUMMARY ** Criminal Law The panel vacated the sentence imposed on Vincent Petrushkin in a case in which Petrushkin pled guilty to possession of a firearm as a felon in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(2), and remanded for resentencing. On appeal, Petrushkin challenged the district court’s application of an enhancement pursuant to U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1), a cross-reference provision that allows courts to apply the base level and special offense characteristics from another substantive offense “[i]f the defendant used or possessed any firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction in connection with the commission or attempted commission of another offense, or possessed or transferred a firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction with knowledge or intent that it would be used or possessed in connection with another offense.” The panel held that the appeal waiver in Petrushkin’s plea agreement allowing him to “appeal only the reasonableness of his sentence” did not waive his right to appeal the district court’s application of the (c)(1) enhancement. The panel held that the “potentially emboldened or facilitated” requirement set forth in United States v. Routon, 25 F.3d 815 (9th Cir. 1994) (concerning U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(6)(b)(B)), applies to both clauses of § 2K2.1(c)(1). ** This summary constitutes no part of the opinion of the court. It has been prepared by court staff for the convenience of the reader. USA V. PETRUSHKIN 3 The government must show that the defendant possessed the firearm in a manner that potentially emboldened or facilitated the other offense. Applying that standard to this case in which the other offense was committed not by Petrushkin but by his codefendant Randy Holmes, the panel held that the district court’s use of (c)(1) was an abuse of discretion because the district court, which focused solely on Petrushkin’s knowledge that Holmes was going to commit a robbery, did not find that Petrushkin possessed the firearm in a manner that potentially emboldened or facilitated Holmes’s offense. Nor do the facts in the record permit the necessary inference. COUNSEL Ian L. Garriques (argued), Assistant United States Attorney; Caitlin A. Baunsgard, Attorney; Vanessa R. Waldref, United States Attorney; Office of the United States Attorney, United States Department of Justice, Spokane, Washington; for Plaintiff-Appellee. Zachary L. Ayers (argued), Ayers Law Firm PLLC, Spokane, Washington, for Defendant-Appellant. 4 USA V. PETRUSHKIN OPINION SUNG, Circuit Judge: The question presented in this case is whether mere possession of a firearm is sufficient to trigger the application of United States Sentencing Guideline (“U.S.S.G.”) § 2K2.1(c)(1). We hold that it is not, and we vacate and remand for resentencing. I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND Randy Holmes told a confidential informant for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (“ATF”) that he needed a gun to conduct a robbery, and ATF set up a sting firearm transaction at a Motel 6 in Spokane on November 5, 2021. Holmes drove to the Motel 6 with William Burns and Vincent Petrushkin (the defendant here). Petrushkin believed that they would rob someone at the Motel 6 but did not know about Holmes’s plan to obtain a gun to conduct future robberies. At the Motel 6, Holmes told Burns and Petrushkin that he was “gonna do this by myself homie” and rejected their offers of help. Burns then gave Holmes a Glock Model 17 9mm semi-automatic handgun. After Burns transferred the gun to Holmes, Petrushkin asked if he could see the gun. Petrushkin “held the gun, looked at it and said hell yeah,” handed the gun back to Holmes, and got into the backseat of the car. Petrushkin possessed the gun for approximately five seconds. Holmes then entered the undercover ATF agent’s car, pointed the Glock at the agent’s head, and demanded a firearm. When the agent told him it was in the back of the car, Holmes exited the vehicle to locate the firearm. The agent got out of the car and told Holmes to drop his weapon. USA V. PETRUSHKIN 5 Holmes shot the agent multiple times, wounding him. Burns and Petrushkin left the scene when the shooting began. Petrushkin was arrested and charged with possession of a firearm as a felon in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(2). He pled guilty and agreed to waive his right to appeal his conviction and sentence if the term of incarceration imposed was less than 12 months and one day. If the court imposed a higher sentence, he reserved the right to appeal “only the reasonableness of his sentence.” Petrushkin’s plea agreement with the government recommended a four-level increase to his base offense level under U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B). The (b)(6)(B) enhancement applies when a defendant “used or possessed any firearm or ammunition in connection with another felony offense; or possessed or transferred any firearm or ammunition with knowledge, intent, or reason to believe that it would be used or possessed in connection with another felony offense.” U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B). At sentencing, the district court applied a different sentencing enhancement, U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1), over Petrushkin’s objection. Section 2K2.1(c)(1) allows courts to apply the base offense level and special offense characteristics from another substantive offense “[i]f the defendant used or possessed any firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction in connection with the commission or attempted commission of another offense, or possessed or transferred a firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction with knowledge or intent that it would be used or possessed in connection with another offense.” U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1). Applying the (c)(1) enhancement, the district court used the robbery base offense level as the starting point for Petrushkin’s Sentencing Guidelines 6 USA V. PETRUSHKIN calculation, resulting in a Guidelines range of 110 to 120 months. In the alternative, the court applied the (b)(6)(B) enhancement and calculated a 77 to 96-month Guideline range. Consistent with the plea agreement, the government requested a sentence of 12 months and one day. The defense requested a sentence of time served, plus ten to twenty days to allow Petrushkin to finalize a community reentry plan. The court sentenced Petrushkin to 48 months in prison and three years of supervised release, and Petrushkin timely appealed. We have jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and 18 U.S.C. § 3742, and we vacate the sentence and remand for resentencing. II. DISCUSSION A. Scope of Appeal Waiver To begin, we must determine whether Petrushkin waived his right to appeal the district court’s application of the (c)(1) enhancement when calculating his Guidelines range. Petrushkin’s plea agreement included an appeal waiver that allowed him to “appeal only the reasonableness of his sentence.” The government argues that the calculation of a Guidelines range implicates only procedural reasonableness, and that Petrushkin’s plea agreement allows him to challenge only the substantive reasonableness of his sentence. We review a defendant’s waiver of his right to appeal de novo, United States v. Bibler, 495 F.3d 621, 623 (9th Cir. 2007), and we reject the government’s argument for two reasons. First, the calculation of a defendant’s Guidelines range implicates both procedural and substantive reasonableness. See Gall v. United States, 552 U.S. 38, 51 (2007) (calculating the incorrect Guidelines range constitutes procedural error); United States v. Carty, 520 F.3d 984, 993 USA V. PETRUSHKIN 7 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc) (instructing courts to “consider the totality of the circumstances, including the degree of variance for a sentence imposed outside the Guidelines range” when evaluating substantive reasonableness). Second, even if the correct application of the Guidelines were strictly a matter of procedural reasonableness, the government’s argument would fail because Petrushkin’s plea agreement allows him to appeal the “reasonableness” of his sentence without any express limitation. That is, the plea agreement does not say that Petrushkin may appeal only the substantive reasonableness of his sentence, nor does it delineate between procedural and substantive review. The reference to “reasonableness,” without limitation, plainly incorporates both the procedural and substantive aspects of reasonableness. And even if the scope of the carve-out in the appeal waiver were ambiguous, we would construe that ambiguity against the government. See United States v. Lo, 839 F.3d 777, 785 (9th Cir. 2016) (noting that because courts “construe plea agreements according to the principles of contract law . . . any ambiguities in the contract language are construed against the drafter, which in this case is the government”). Because Petrushkin’s plea agreement allows him to challenge the district court’s Guidelines calculation, we turn to the merits of his argument that the district court erred when it applied the (c)(1) enhancement to his sentence. B. Application of U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1) We review the district court’s legal interpretation of the Sentencing Guidelines de novo. United States v. Holt, 510 F.3d 1007, 1010 (9th Cir. 2007). We review the

Applying that standard to this case in which the other offense was committed not by Petrushkin but by his codefendant Randy Holmes, the panel held that the district court’s use of (c)(1) was an abuse of discretion because the district court, which focused solely on Petrushkin’s knowledge that Holmes was going to commit a robbery, did not find that Petrushkin possessed the firearm in a manner that potentially emboldened or facilitated Holmes’s offense. PETRUSHKIN OPINION SUNG, Circuit Judge: The question presented in this case is whether mere possession of a firearm is sufficient to trigger the application of United States Sentencing Guideline (“U.S.S.G.”) § 2K2.1(c)(1). We hold that it is not, and we vacate and remand for resentencing. I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND Randy Holmes told a confidential informant for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (“ATF”) that he needed a gun to conduct a robbery, and ATF set up a sting firearm transaction at a Motel 6 in Spokane on November 5, 2021. Holmes drove to the Motel 6 with William Burns and Vincent Petrushkin (the defendant here). Petrushkin believed that they would rob someone at the Motel 6 but did not know about Holmes’s plan to obtain a gun to conduct future robberies. At the Motel 6, Holmes told Burns and Petrushkin that he was “gonna do this by myself homie” and rejected their offers of help. Burns then gave Holmes a Glock Model 17 9mm semi-automatic handgun. After Burns transferred the gun to Holmes, Petrushkin asked if he could see the gun. Petrushkin “held the gun, looked at it and said hell yeah,” handed the gun back to Holmes, and got into the backseat of the car. Petrushkin possessed the gun for approximately five seconds. Holmes then entered the undercover ATF agent’s car, pointed the Glock at the agent’s head, and demanded a firearm. When the agent told him it was in the back of the car, Holmes exited the vehicle to locate the firearm. The agent got out of the car and told Holmes to drop his weapon. USA V. PETRUSHKIN 5 Holmes shot the agent multiple times, wounding him. Burns and Petrushkin left the scene when the shooting began. Petrushkin was arrested and charged with possession of a firearm as a felon in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(2). He pled guilty and agreed to waive his right to appeal his conviction and sentence if the term of incarceration imposed was less than 12 months and one day. If the court imposed a higher sentence, he reserved the right to appeal “only the reasonableness of his sentence.” Petrushkin’s plea agreement with the government recommended a four-level increase to his base offense level under U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B). The (b)(6)(B) enhancement applies when a defendant “used or possessed any firearm or ammunition in connection with another felony offense; or possessed or transferred any firearm or ammunition with knowledge, intent, or reason to believe that it would be used or possessed in connection with another felony offense.” U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B). At sentencing, the district court applied a different sentencing enhancement, U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1), over Petrushkin’s objection. Section 2K2.1(c)(1) allows courts to apply the base offense level and special offense characteristics from another substantive offense “[i]f the defendant used or possessed any firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction in connection with the commission or attempted commission of another offense, or possessed or transferred a firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction with knowledge or intent that it would be used or possessed in connection with another offense.” U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1). Applying the (c)(1) enhancement, the district court used the robbery base offense level as the starting point for Petrushkin’s Sentencing Guidelines 6 USA V. PETRUSHKIN calculation, resulting in a Guidelines range of 110 to 120 months. In the alternative, the court applied the (b)(6)(B) enhancement and calculated a 77 to 96-month Guideline range. Consistent with the plea agreement, the government requested a sentence of 12 months and one day. The defense requested a sentence of time served, plus ten to twenty days to allow Petrushkin to finalize a community reentry plan. The court sentenced Petrushkin to 48 months in prison and three years of supervised release, and Petrushkin timely appealed. We have jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and 18 U.S.C. § 3742, and we vacate the sentence and remand for resentencing. II. DISCUSSION A. Scope of Appeal Waiver To begin, we must determine whether Petrushkin waived his right to appeal the district court’s application of the (c)(1) enhancement when calculating his Guidelines range. Petrushkin’s plea agreement included an appeal waiver that allowed him to “appeal only the reasonableness of his sentence.” The government argues that the calculation of a Guidelines range implicates only procedural reasonableness, and that Petrushkin’s plea agreement allows him to challenge only the substantive reasonableness of his sentence. We review a defendant’s waiver of his right to appeal de novo, United States v. Bibler, 495 F.3d 621, 623 (9th Cir. 2007), and we reject the government’s argument for two reasons. First, the calculation of a defendant’s Guidelines range implicates both procedural and substantive reasonableness. See Gall v. United States, 552 U.S. 38, 51 (2007) (calculating the incorrect Guidelines range constitutes procedural error); United States v. Carty, 520 F.3d 984, 993 USA V. PETRUSHKIN 7 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc) (instructing courts to “consider the totality of the circumstances, including the degree of variance for a sentence imposed outside the Guidelines range” when evaluating substantive reasonableness). Second, even if the correct application of the Guidelines were strictly a matter of procedural reasonableness, the government’s argument would fail because Petrushkin’s plea agreement allows him to appeal the “reasonableness” of his sentence without any express limitation. That is, the plea agreement does not say that Petrushkin may appeal only the substantive reasonableness of his sentence, nor does it delineate between procedural and substantive review. The reference to “reasonableness,” without limitation, plainly incorporates both the procedural and substantive aspects of reasonableness. And even if the scope of the carve-out in the appeal waiver were ambiguous, we would construe that ambiguity against the government. See United States v. Lo, 839 F.3d 777, 785 (9th Cir. 2016) (noting that because courts “construe plea agreements according to the principles of contract law . . . any ambiguities in the contract language are construed against the drafter, which in this case is the government”). Because Petrushkin’s plea agreement allows him to challenge the district court’s Guidelines calculation, we turn to the merits of his argument that the district court erred when it applied the (c)(1) enhancement to his sentence. B. Application of U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1) We review the district court’s legal interpretation of the Sentencing Guidelines de novo. United States v. Holt, 510 F.3d 1007, 1010 (9th Cir. 2007).
